extracted.intended_audience: educated literary readers (19th-century readers of Sartor Resartus); readers interested in philosophy of clothes, social satire, and cultural critique
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative statements, prescriptive rules, and descriptive criteria embedded in Carlyle's Sartor Resartus chapter about Custom, Wonder, Space/Time, and the sects of Dandies and Poor-Slaves (including the explicit 'Articles of Faith').

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge Custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom is the greatest of Weavers; we do everything by Custom; Philosophy is throughout a continual battle against Custom, an ever-renewed effort to transcend the sphere of blind Custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage argues that many of our axioms are unexamined habits inculcated by Custom; philosophical work consists in recognizing and attempting to transcend these customary assumptions. Examples: beliefs we have 'never heard questioned'; Custom 'hoodwinked us'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing repetition to dull your sense of wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Innumerable are the illusions and legerdemain-tricks of Custom: but of all these, perhaps the cleverest is her knack of persuading us that the Miraculous, by simple repetition, ceases to be Miraculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the Stupendous with indifference simply because you have seen it many times. Carlyle contrasts a living mind with a mere 'Work-Machine' whose powers are merely functional—implying a normative injunction to preserve wonder and attention in contemplation of extraordinary phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that names and classifications can obscure phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable enough too ... wilt thou find the potency of Names; which indeed are but one kind of such custom-woven, wonder-hiding Garments. Witchcraft ... we have now named Madness, and Diseases of the Nerves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the reader to question whether terminological labels (e.g., 'madness', 'disease') have disguised the original mystery; the advice is to see through names-as-clothes to the underlying reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Space and Time as thought-forms that can hide the transcendent
rubrics_metrics.description: Your two grand fundamental world-enveloping Appearances, SPACE and TIME ... lie all-embracing, as the universal canvas, or warp and woof, whereby all minor Illusions ... weave and paint themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle advises that Space and Time condition and determine our practical reasonings and imagings but should not be allowed to usurp pure spiritual meditation; he uses imaginative devices (e.g., Fortunatus's hats) to illustrate how annihilating space or time would unmask miracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use memory and hope (inner faculties) to commune with past and future
rubrics_metrics.description: Those mystic faculties of thine, Memory and Hope, already answer: already through those mystic avenues ... the curtains of Yesterday drop down, the curtains of To-morrow roll up; but Yesterday and To-morrow both are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats Memory and Hope as legitimate means to experience past and future 'as present'—a prescriptive point about spiritual/intellectual practice: cultivate inward faculties to access a kind of immortality or eternal present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit Space and Time as Forms but do not overrealize them
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit Space and Time to their due rank as Forms of Thought; nay even, if thou wilt, to their quite undue rank of Realities: and consider, then, with thyself how their thin disguises hide from us the brightest God-effulgences!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical stance: allow practical use of space/time concepts, but remain critical of treating them as absolute realities that obscure spiritual truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Dandy
rubrics_metrics.description: A Dandy is a Clothes-wearing Man, a Man whose trade, office and existence consists in the wearing of Clothes. Every faculty of his soul, spirit, purse and person is heroically consecrated to this one object, the wearing of Clothes wisely and well: so that as others dress to live, he lives to dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle gives a behavioural/identity criterion: Dandyism is complete devotion of one's faculties to the art of dress; it is aesthetic and devotional rather than economic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dandy's desired recompense: recognition by the gaze
rubrics_metrics.description: But, for all this ... what is it that the Dandy asks in return? Solely, we may say, that you would recognize his existence; would admit him to be a living object; or even failing this, a visual object ... do but look at him, and he is contented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative note on social purpose of dandying: the dandy's legitimate aim is visual acknowledgment and understanding, not monetary reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dandiacal Sect's institutional features
rubrics_metrics.description: They affect great purity and separatism; distinguish themselves by a particular costume; likewise, so far as possible, by a particular speech; They have their Temples ... named Almack's; They worship principally by night; and have their High-priests and High-priestesses ... The rites ... are held strictly secret. Nor are Sacred Books wanting to the Sect; these they call Fashionable Novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the organizational and ritual criteria that mark the Dandiacal body: costume, speech, temples, nocturnal worship, secret rites, and a canon (fashionable novels) with canonical vs non-canonical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dandiacal sect as religious/self-worship (diagnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: To my own surmise, it appears as if this Dandiacal Sect were but a new modification, adapted to the new time, of that primeval Superstition, Self-worship; ... if any one chooses to name it revived Ahrimanism, or a new figure of Demon-Worship, I have, so far as is yet visible, no objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion: interpret Dandyism as a quasi-religious phenomenon (fetish-worship, hero-worship, or self-worship) rather than mere fashion; the passage provides a critical lens for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Coats and wrinkles
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Coats should have nothing of the triangle about them; at the same time, wrinkles behind should be carefully avoided.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Dandiacal 'Confession of Faith' quoted literally; Carlyle (or the Professor) signals his own denial, but reproduces the sartorial prescription verbatim as an authoritative rule within the sect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Collar rule
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The collar is a very important point: it should be low behind, and slightly rolled.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit sartorial prescription from the Dandiacal 'Articles of Faith' regarding collar shape and turning; presented as canonical guidance for proper dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Avoid 'posterial luxuriance'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No license of fashion can allow a man of delicate taste to adopt the posterial luxuriance of a Hottentot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sartorial prohibition (pejorative and period-specific) presented as a rule of taste within the Dandiacal code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Safety in a swallow-tail
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is safety in a swallow-tail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise sartorial maxim asserting preference for the swallow-tail coat as a mark of secure taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Rings as sign of good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The good sense of a gentleman is nowhere more finely developed than in his rings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive claim that choice of rings is a refined indicator of gentlemanly judgment—part of the Dandiacal evaluative code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: White waistcoats permitted with restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is permitted to mankind, under certain restrictions, to wear white waistcoats.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional sartorial permission: white waistcoats are allowed but subject to unspecified restrictions—an encoded rule about acceptable forms of dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Faith: Trousers fit
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The trousers must be exceedingly tight across the hips.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rule prescribing extremely tight trousers across the hips as a required element of the Dandiacal silhouette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor-Slaves (Drudge) sect vows and social rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poor-Slaves (also called Drudges, White Negroes, Ragged-Beggars, Hallanshakers, etc.) appear bound by the Monastic Vows of Poverty and Obedience (observed with great strictness, sometimes pledged before birth); they wear a peculiar costume of innumerable skirts, lappets and irregular wings fastened by buttons, thrums and skewers, often with a girdle of leather or straw rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive-prescriptive overview of membership criteria for this sect: vows, early consecration, and distinctive costume constitute the identity and behavioral rules of the Poor-Slaves community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor-Slaves dietary and drinking prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of diet, all Poor-Slaves are Rhizophagous (root-eaters); a few are Ichthyophagous and use Salted Herrings; their universal sustenance is the root named Potato, cooked by fire alone, with an unknown condiment named 'Point'. For drink they use Milk and 'Potheen' (a pungent homemade spirit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific alimentary rules: primary reliance on potatoes and potheen in religious observances; drinking potheen is indicated as indispensable in their solemnities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor-Slaves habitus and practices (Druidic/Earth-worship features)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poor-Slaves live in dark dwellings, sometimes break windows and stuff them with raiment to restore 'fit obscurity'; they dig and work in the earth, meditate/manipulate earth substances, and are liable to out-breakings of enthusiasm rising to ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral and environmental norms: their living conditions, propensity for obscurity, earth-focused labor, and potential for violent enthusiasm are described as characteristic rules/practices of the sect.
